entry.title: Test before you trust: what a GNN adds to outage screening, and where it stops

link.title: Test before you trust: what a GNN adds to outage screening, and where it stops

entry.content:
TL;DR. On a standard test grid I asked how many exact outage calculations a screen can safely skip. The plain physics shortcut with one correction skips 73.7 % of them. A graph neural network adds about 5-7 points on top. Off familiar ground the learned screen misses more than its target allows. Fix the baseline first, then test off familiar ground.

Why this matters

A grid operator needs to know what would happen if one single line trips (background). The rule, called N-1, is that the grid must then stay within its limits. So you take a solved state of the grid, remove the lines one by one, and each time recompute it and look for overloads.

The exact check is one full grid calculation per outage. This test grid has 186 branches (lines and transformers), so that many exact calculations for one operating state. A screen sorts the outages first. Clearly safe ones are skipped; the rest get the exact calculation.

Below, one line fails. The exact calculation puts another well above its limit; the plain shortcut, a simple estimate, reads it below.

A selected example, not a typical one. Line 65-68 fails; the exact calculation puts line 49-69 at 127 %, the plain shortcut at 97 % (before its safety margin). Blue: the GNN.

The question is how good that sorting can be.

The question, and what I expected

I asked how many exact runs a screen can skip while it still catches 99 of 100 overloaded cases: the target. A case is one operating state with one outage; it is overloaded if the exact calculation puts any remaining branch above its rating. I also asked how much of that is learning and how much plain physics.

I come from machine learning, not from power engineering. I learned the grid side for this project, out of interest in grids that carry more renewable power. A grid is a graph, so I expected a graph neural network (GNN) to be expressive enough to capture the non-linear physics the plain shortcut misses. I also expected it to struggle on patterns it never saw in training, where deep learning often breaks. So the plan included tests off familiar ground, meaning load levels and outages unlike those in training.

The setup in one picture

On a standard test grid I made synthetic operating states (random load levels, cost-optimised generation) and solved every outage exactly, as the reference.

The plain shortcut is a simplified linear calculation. It uses fixed factors that say how a failed branch’s flow moves onto the other branches. The corrected shortcut adds one simple correction. A plain neural network sees the grid as a flat list of numbers; the GNN sees nodes joined by branches and learns a correction to the plain shortcut.

One case is one operating state with one outage. The screen sends a case to the exact calculation when its worst estimate plus the safety margin crosses 100 %.

Each screen gets one safety margin, an offset added to every estimate, set on held-back states so that the target is met there. No held-back or test state was used for training. The target is not a guarantee: the margin is calibrated for it, and only for cases like the held-back states. Then I count the exact runs skipped: how sharp a screen is, not time saved.

What worked

A perfect screen, which sends on only the real overloads and the outages that split the grid, could skip 79.7 % of the exact runs. The plain shortcut skips only 28.6 %. It is oversimplified: it counts only part of what loads a branch, so it can read too low and needs a wide margin.

That natural gap mostly goes away with one pre-computed ratio. For each branch I divide its exact loading by the shortcut’s loading in the intact grid, limit that ratio to between half and double, and apply it after the outage. No learning. With this one correction the same shortcut skips 73.7 %. I built it after the main results, to check that the baseline was fair. It is my own simple version of a known idea.

The correction assumes the ratio stays the same after the outage. In reality flows redistribute in a more complicated way, which is left to learn. The GNN skips 79.4 %, almost the maximum, with the target met on average over three training runs. Over the corrected shortcut, learning adds about 5-7 points, depending on that limit. Honestly, that is not a big difference.

Exact runs each screen lets you skip on familiar ground, margin set to catch 99 of 100 overloaded cases. Whiskers: three limits for the ratio (corrected shortcut), training runs (networks).

What did not work, and why

Then I left familiar ground: states with higher load than any in training, and unseen outages (branches that never failed in training or calibration, at both load levels).

On unseen outages the GNN caught 95-98 of 100 overloaded cases. At higher load it caught 96 to just under 99, recomputed afterwards without rounding: both short of the target. The plain neural network caught only about 70 on unseen outages. The plain shortcut kept its target, but then skipped very little.

Overloaded cases caught per 100, three training runs of the GNN, margin set on familiar ground. The unseen-outage set includes normal and higher load; higher-load values recomputed afterwards.

One planned test failed too. Networks trained separately should disagree where they are unsure. I had seven screening rules, and most used that disagreement as a warning sign. The rules and the pass mark were written down before the first run. None passed.

The margin can only hold for cases like the ones it was set on. The rest was checked afterwards. The networks did notice that the grid had changed. But where they were wrong, they tended to be wrong together: three copies of one network were off in the same direction. So their disagreement did not point at the misses. The GNN’s missed overloads also got bigger: none more than one point above the limit on familiar ground, some far above it off it.

The take-away

In short: learned approximations can be useful, but be aware of where they apply.

  • Physics first. Fix the baseline before you credit the model.
  • Test before you trust. A calibrated margin is not a guarantee. Off familiar ground a learned screen needs a new test, or a physics fallback.
  • For an operator, a learned screen is a first filter, for ranking outages and for planning studies with many scenarios. It does not replace the security check.

Limits and details

  • One standard test grid. Its line limits and my operating states are synthetic, and the states are not N-1 secure: overloads are far more common than in real operation. I checked overloads only, not voltage or stability.
  • The target is nominal. Cases from one state resemble each other, and even on familiar ground a single training run can land just below it.
  • No speed claim: on a grid this small a fast solver needs a fraction of a second for nearly all outages of a state.

For specialists: the grid is the IEEE 118-bus case, and exact means AC power flow. The plain shortcut is DC power flow with line outage factors; it leaves out reactive power. The margin is set by split conformal calibration. The corrected shortcut follows the hot-start idea of starting from a solved state; I did not compare the established versions. Related work: learned models for grid outages (one, two), a calibrated screen for multiple outages and a screen tested under changing conditions. Nothing here is a new method. Full tables are in RESULTS.md.

Built with pandapower, lightsim2grid and PyTorch Geometric, and with AI coding agents under tests. I chose the question, directed the work and reviewed the results; the headline numbers were recomputed independently with separate code.
entry.summary: On a standard test grid, plain physics with one simple correction closes most of the gap to the exact calculation and a GNN adds a little more, until conditions leave familiar ground.

entry.title: Lose one line: where the linear shortcut fails

link.title: Lose one line: where the linear shortcut fails

entry.content:
TL;DR. A routine task for transmission system operators (TSOs) is to check that losing any one line overloads nothing else. The fast shortcut for this check, DC power flow, comes at a price: it ignores reactive power, so it can underestimate a line’s real loading and miss an overload. On IEEE 30-bus, a small standard test grid, at nominal load and before any outage, DC puts the one overloaded line at 77 %; exact AC power flow puts it at 112 %.

Electricity does not take the route you choose. When a line in a meshed grid trips, its flow jumps onto every parallel path at once, guided by physics. Checking what happens after a failure takes a physics calculation.

My background is in graph machine learning, and I want to know how it can help power grids, which keep growing in importance and complexity. This post is the 101 I worked through first: the N-1 check on IEEE 30-bus, a small standard test grid. The notebook and code are in the companion repo.

N-1: lose one line, stay within limits

N-1 is the grid minus any one element, for example a line. The N-1 criterion says the grid must stay within its limits after every such outage: no line above its rating, no voltage outside its band. Operators check this in advance, and if an outage would overload another line, they act before it happens. A common remedy is shifting generation (redispatch).

A toy grid. Dots are buses, the points where generators, loads and lines connect; ~ marks a generator. Every line is rated 65 MW, and arrow width is MW. When the top line trips, the middle line goes from 46 % to 104 % of its rating.

After a change in topology, the check looks for the grid’s new steady state: the operating point that satisfies the power flow equations, which balance the power injected and consumed at every bus. Those equations are nonlinear in the bus voltages and angles.

A small grid with one weak corridor

IEEE 30-bus serves 189 MW, and its generators could produce 335 MW. Supply is not the problem; line capacity in the right place is.

Lines coloured by AC loading at nominal load, light grey (empty) to near-black (full); red is above 100 %. Triangles: generators; square: slack bus, which balances the rest.

Bus 8, near the top, is the largest load: 30 MW plus 30 Mvar of reactive power (more on that below). The original IEEE case had a synchronous condenser there, a machine that supplies only reactive power; this version of the data dropped it. So bus 8’s reactive demand comes in mostly over line 6-8, which is at 112 % before anything fails. A what-if in the notebook confirms the cause: a 30 Mvar capacitor at bus 8, which supplies most of its reactive demand on site, brings the line down to 79 %, while the line’s active power barely changes (24.8 to 24.9 MW). What overloads the line is not the MW. It is the reactive power.

Three kinds of power in one wire

A line is limited by heat, and heat comes from current. Active power P does work. Reactive power Q moves back and forth every cycle to build the magnetic fields of motors and transformers. It delivers no net energy, but it is real current and heats the wire just the same.

The two parts of the current are 90° apart in phase, so they add like perpendicular vectors. The apparent power S, which sets the total current, is the hypotenuse: S² = P² + Q². What actually limits a line is heat, so its real limit is a current, in amperes. Grid engineers prefer to work in power units, and at a fixed voltage current is proportional to S. So line ratings are given in MVA: a current limit expressed in power units, with P and Q both counting toward it.

Line 6-8 at nominal load, to scale. Grey: P, the only part DC power flow keeps. Orange: Q. Black: S. Dashed red arc: the 32 MVA rating.

Line 6-8 carries 24.8 MW and 24.4 Mvar. The MW alone fit inside the 32 MVA rating; together they make about 35 MVA, outside it.pandapower reports loading as current over rated current. Bus 8 sits at 0.961 p.u. (per unit: voltage as a fraction of its nominal value), so the same MVA takes a little more current, and the AC loading of 112 % is a bit higher than 35 ÷ 32. Heat grows with the square of the current, so the reactive part causes 49 % of this line’s heat loss.

This part took me a while to figure out. I first read MW, Mvar and MVA as three quantities that should not be added. They are one unit, volts times amperes, under three labels. P and Q come from the in-phase and the 90° parts of the same current, which is why they add like the sides of a right triangle.

The linear shortcut reads low

Exact AC power flow solves the nonlinear power flow equations for the unknown bus voltages and angles with an iterative numerical method, usually Newton-Raphson, repeated until it converges. DC power flow makes four simplifying assumptions (flat voltages, small angles, no resistance, no reactive power) and turns them into a system of linear equations, solved cheaply in a single step. That is why it is the fast screening tool in practice: operators precompute sensitivity tables on it and screen thousands of outages at once.

DC gets the MW nearly right: on this grid it is off by 0.39 MW per line on average. With voltage fixed and Q gone, MVA and MW become the same number, so DC divides its MW by the MVA rating and calls that loading. The real limit is on current, and current includes Q.

The 12 of 41 lines where DC is furthest from AC, at nominal load. Black: AC; grey: DC; dashed red: the limit. Orange bars: reactive share Q/S.

On line 6-8, AC says 112 % and DC says 77 %: “fine” for the one line that is overloaded. Over all 41 lines DC reads only 6.3 points low on average. Its errors sit on lines with a large reactive share (70 % on 6-8), and those include the two most loaded lines, 6-8 and 21-22 (95 % in AC, 64 % in DC).

Scanning all 41 outages

This is where the shortcut has to earn its place: one fast pass over every outage. An N-1 scan takes each line out in turn and checks every limit. I ran it at 80 % load, because at full load line 6-8 is over its rating before any outage.

One column per outage at 0.8× load. Top: worst AC line loading after the trip (dot) and the DC estimate (grey dash). Bottom: lowest bus voltage. Colour: why the outage is critical.

7 of the 41 outages are critical:

  • Thermal (red), 2. Losing 6-8 pushes 8-28 to 118 %; losing 8-28 pushes 6-8 to 110 %.
  • Voltage only (violet), 4. A bus drops below 0.95 p.u. Losing 6-8 does that too, on top of its overload.
  • Islanding (hollow), 1. Losing 25-26 cuts off bus 26.

Here is the lesson. DC sees both thermal outages, but places the surviving line below its limit both times, so a thermal screen that trusted it would have passed both. Its overall ranking of outages is decent (rank correlation 0.74 with AC). What it gets wrong is which side of 100 % a line lands on, and for a thermal check that is the deciding question. Fast and usually close is not the same as safe.

How fast security tips over

I repeated the full scan, all 41 outages, at load levels from 0.5× to 1.5× nominal, scaling all loads and generation together. In the figure, each bar is one outage, and its height is the worst loading of any line after that trip. The slider sets the load level.

Interactive. One bar per outage, sorted by severity at 0.8× load; red above 100 %. Grey ticks: the DC estimate for the same outage. Drag the slider to change the load.

Move the slider from 0.85× to 0.9×: thermally critical outages jump from 2 to 19, while the intact grid is still within limits and every grey tick stays below the line. One corridor is already almost fully loaded; once it sits near its limit, almost any redistribution tips it over. DC flags its first overload only at 1.0×, a whole regime late. From 0.95× on, the intact grid itself is over its limit, so every outage counts as critical, trivially.

What comes next

DC power flow gets the MW nearly right in one linear solve. It fails in one place, on lines with large reactive flow near their limit, which is exactly where an N-1 check needs to be right.

In the next post I move to a 118-bus standard test grid and ask the operator’s question directly: how much of the exact AC work can a screen skip without missing overloads? It compares the operator’s linear shortcut, a simple physics correction of it, and a graph neural network.

The next post is out: Test before you trust: what a GNN adds to outage screening, and where it stops.

Built with pandapower (AC and DC power flow, and the IEEE 30-bus case), marimo notebooks, NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib and Plotly, in a uv-pinned environment with pytest in CI. Thanks to the pandapower team for making grid analysis this accessible. Code written with AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex) in a test-guided loop; results reviewed and every number checked against its source.
entry.summary: N-1 security, AC vs DC power flow, and why reactive power hides overloads, on a small standard test grid.
